summary: Uthman ibn Affan (RA) was the third of the Rightly Guided Caliphs and a companion of singular distinction — the only person to have married two daughters of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ sequentially, earning him the title Dhul-Nurayn (Possessor of Two Lights). A wealthy merchant of great generosity, he financed major campaigns and projects for early Islam, and his caliphate saw the standardization of the Quran's written text — a legacy that endures to this day.
biography:
Uthman ibn Affan ibn Abi al-As al-Umawi al-Qurashi was born around 576 CE in Makkah, into the Banu Umayyah clan of Quraysh — one of the most prominent and wealthy clans among the Arabs. He was approximately six years younger than the Prophet ﷺ. Before Islam, he was a successful merchant known for his refined character, modesty, and generosity — qualities unusual in the competitive mercantile culture of pre-Islamic Makkah.

Uthman accepted Islam early in the Prophet's mission, among the first ten or twelve converts, after being called to the faith by Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA). His uncle Hakam ibn Abi al-As, distressed at his conversion, bound him and pressured him to recant — but Uthman refused. The Prophet ﷺ recognized his character and gave him his daughter Ruqayyah bint Muhammad in marriage, an honor that set him apart from the beginning of his Islamic life.

When persecution in Makkah intensified, Uthman was among the first Muslims to emigrate to Abyssinia, taking his wife Ruqayyah with him in the first emigration to the court of the Negus (al-Najashi). He returned to Makkah when reports (later proven false) spread that the Quraysh had accepted Islam, and subsequently emigrated again. Ibn Sa'd records in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra that the Prophet ﷺ referred to him and his wife Ruqayyah as having made a twin emigration echoing that of Ibrahim (AS) and his family.

Ruqayyah bint Muhammad died while Uthman was in Madinah, on the day of the Battle of Badr (2 AH), which is why Uthman was not present at the battle — he had remained at her bedside by the Prophet's instruction. The Prophet ﷺ then gave him his other daughter, Umm Kulthum bint Muhammad (RA), in marriage — making Uthman unique in Islamic history as the son-in-law of the Prophet ﷺ through two of his daughters. It is for this reason that he was given the title Dhul-Nurayn (possessor of two lights). When Umm Kulthum also died (9 AH), the Prophet ﷺ reportedly said: 'If I had a third daughter, I would have given her to Uthman.' (al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, Ibn Sa'd)

Uthman's financial generosity to the early Muslim community was extraordinary. When the Muslims prepared for the expedition to Tabuk (9 AH) — an arduous campaign requiring provisions for a large army against Byzantine-backed forces in a time of drought — the Prophet ﷺ called on the Sahaba to contribute. Uthman came forward with 300 camels fully equipped, 1,000 gold dinars, and 50 horses. The Prophet ﷺ took the coins in his hands and said: 'Nothing that Uthman does after today will harm him.' (Sunan al-Tirmidhi, graded hasan; al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, Vol. 3). He also purchased the well of Rumah from a Jewish man and donated it as a waqf (endowment) for the Muslim community of Madinah when they were suffering water scarcity — recorded by al-Bukhari in al-Tarikh al-Kabir and referenced in Musnad al-Bazzar.

He was selected as third Caliph by the six-member shura council appointed by Umar ibn al-Khattab before his death. His caliphate (23–35 AH / 644–656 CE) lasted twelve years — the longest of the four Rightly Guided Caliphs. The first six years are described in classical sources as peaceful and prosperous, marked by continued expansion: into North Africa, Cyprus, parts of Central Asia, and further consolidation in Persia. The later years saw growing internal discord, which classical historians record carefully without taking sectarian sides.

The most enduring achievement of Uthman's caliphate was the standardization and distribution of the Quran's written text. Recognizing that variations in recitation had begun to cause disputes as Islam spread to non-Arab populations, Uthman established a committee under Zayd ibn Thabit — assisted by Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, Sa'id ibn al-As, and Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith — to compile a master codex from Abu Bakr's original compilation. Copies were made and sent to the major centers of the Muslim world (Makkah, Madinah, Basrah, Kufah, and Syria), and regional variant manuscripts were collected and destroyed. This decisive action — unanimously accepted by the surviving major Sahaba — standardized the Quran's text and is one of the greatest services rendered to the preservation of the divine revelation. (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab Fada'il al-Quran; al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, Ibn Sa'd, Vol. 3)

In the final years of his caliphate, Uthman faced organized opposition from groups in Egypt, Kufah, and Basrah who objected to his appointment of relatives from Banu Umayyah as governors — a governance decision about which classical scholars have offered varied analysis. The crisis culminated in 35 AH (656 CE), when rebels besieged his home in Madinah for approximately forty days. Uthman refused to authorize armed defense, fearing Muslim bloodshed, and was killed while reading the Quran — drops of his blood, according to multiple narrations, fell on the ayah: 'So Allah will suffice you against them; He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.' (Quran 2:137).

The events surrounding his death and the subsequent civil war (fitna) are among the most discussed in Islamic history. Classical Sunni scholarship — following the methodology of Ibn Taymiyyah in Minhaj al-Sunnah and al-Dhahabi in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' — holds that all major figures involved were Muslims acting on their best judgment in a deeply complicated situation; none are condemned as apostates, and none should be cursed. The matter is referred to the judgment of Allah.

Uthman was buried in Madinah, and his grave is in the Baqi cemetery. The Prophet ﷺ gave glad tidings of paradise to Uthman on multiple occasions, and all Sunni scholars are unanimous in affirming his station as one of the foremost of the Sahaba.

key_events.event: Accepted Islam among the first converts, through Abu Bakr al-Siddiq
Emigrated to Abyssinia (first emigration) with his wife Ruqayyah bint Muhammad
Remained at the bedside of his dying wife Ruqayyah; not present at Badr
Married Umm Kulthum bint Muhammad ﷺ after Ruqayyah's death — titled Dhul-Nurayn
Donated 300 camels, 1,000 dinars, and 50 horses for the Tabuk expedition
Donated well of Rumah as waqf for the Muslim community of Madinah
Selected as third Caliph by the shura council
Expeditions into North Africa and Cyprus
Standardized the Quran text; distributed Uthmani codices to major cities
Besieged in his home for forty days by rebels; martyred while reciting the Quran

notable_traits: Extreme modesty and shyness — the Prophet ﷺ noted that even the angels were shy before Uthman
Extraordinary financial generosity for the cause of Islam
Consistent devotion to recitation and memorization of the Quran
Non-confrontational and forbearing by nature — refused to allow armed defense even when his life was threatened
Son-in-law of the Prophet ﷺ through two marriages
